title: Fortitude (ST II-II.123)
hook: courage is mostly endurance, not attack

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice: a steady will to give each person, and God, their due. Your line was each their due.

Two kinds of brave. The first runs into the burning building. It's sudden, loud, and it makes the evening news. The second sits in a plastic chair beside a hospital bed through a long night, and the next, and the next. Nobody films it. There's nothing to charge at, only staying. Ask the evening news which one is courage, and the first one wins. Ask Thomas Aquinas, and you get a different answer. After prudence and justice comes the third of the cardinal virtues. Fortitude.
screen: `THE BURNING BUILDING.` → `THE PLASTIC CHAIR, NIGHT AFTER NIGHT.` → `WHICH ONE IS COURAGE?`

segments.voice: Fortitude, for Thomas, keeps a person steady in the good when fear pushes them to quit. It deals with two things: fear, which makes us want to run, and daring, which can make us reckless. Fortitude holds the line between them. Then his surprising claim. Its main act isn't attacking. It's enduring: standing firm. His reasons: when you attack, you're usually the stronger one in that moment; when you endure, something stronger is pressing on you. Attack looks to a danger still ahead; endurance faces one already here. And attack can be over in a flash, while endurance has to last. So staying is often harder than charging. The plastic chair, not the burning building. Thomas has in mind above all the gravest dangers, standing firm even before death, and he calls martyrdom the highest act of this virtue. The Catechism describes fortitude more broadly, as firmness in difficulties and constancy in pursuing the good. That widens it to ordinary life: the long illness, the job you can't leave yet, the child who isn't sleeping, the grief that won't hurry. Jesus says in the Douay-Rheims: "but he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved." Persevere. Not win. Last. And fortitude isn't the absence of fear. Thomas assumes the fear is there; that's what the virtue is for. A person with fortitude feels the full weight, and doesn't put down the good thing they're carrying.
screen: `STEADY WHEN FEAR SAYS QUIT.` · `THE MAIN ACT IS ENDURING.` · `STAYING IS HARDER THAN CHARGING.` · `NOT FEARLESS: FAITHFUL.` · then, large: `HE THAT SHALL PERSEVERE UNTO THE END.`

segments.voice: Name one hard thing you're carrying that won't be fixed today, a worry, a body that hurts, a season lasting too long, and breathe beside it the way someone sits beside a hospital bed, letting the urge to run into distraction or anger come, and staying anyway. If you pray, ask God for strength for today only.
Fortitude. For Thomas, the steadiness to hold to the good in the face of fear, whose main act is enduring, not attacking. Today's word.
Your line: endure. Not fearless, but faithful, carrying the good thing under its full weight. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching counts fortitude among the four cardinal virtues and among the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and Catholics honor the martyrs as its highest witnesses while also praying for strength in illness, grief and ordinary trials.

chat.meaning: For Thomas, fortitude holds firm in the good despite fear. Enduring is harder than attacking: it faces a danger already here, and it has to last.

cardinal virtues.meaning: the four hinge virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance

martyrdom.meaning: dying as a witness to the faith

Catechism.meaning: the Catholic Church's official summary of its teaching

sources.quoted: but he that shall persevere unto the end, he shall be saved.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: fortitude concerns fear and daring (II-II.123.3); chiefly about dangers of death (II-II.123.4); the principal act is endurance rather than attack, with three reasons (a stronger opponent, present rather than future danger, long duration) (II-II.123.6 ad 1); martyrdom as the most perfect act of fortitude (II-II.124.3).
The Catechism's broader description (firmness in difficulties, constancy in pursuing the good) is paraphrased from CCC 1808.
howItsDone says fortitude is among the gifts of the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 11:2 in the Vulgate tradition; CCC 1831); confirm.
